text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- An opinion poll shows that the ruling Social Democrats and conserative opposition the Moderates both need the support of the greens in parliament to retain power in next year's general election. The two biggest parties are neck-to-neck in the polls with the Social Democrats having 33.5 percent of support and Moderates 32.5 percent.

- Up to 52,000 new jobs will be created next year, according to estimates by the Labour Market Board. The board said there had been improvements in all sectors in 1997 and the outlook for 1998 looked good. Bosse Ringholm has been appointed the new general director for the board, Arbetsmarknadstyrelsen (AMS).

- S-E-Banken has lost three of the company's four senior people over the past two years to the corporate finance area. The latest to go is Richard Josephson who has left for EQT, Investor's risk capital company.

- Sweden can become a safe haven for foreign capital after having decided to stay outside Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU). Overseas interest has increased since Sweden decided not to join EMU at the start in 1999. Swedish debt yields have fallen most in Europe together with Spanish and Italian yields. The gap between Swedish and German long bond yields has fallen to under one percent. The crown has firmed against the mark and dollar.
- Swedish mining equipment firm Svedala has won a record order from Iran's state mining company worth 700 million crowns.
- Clothing company Lindex saw its sales rise 10 percent from September 1996 to May this year to 2.22 million crowns. Pre-tax profit rose by 58 percent to 166 million crowns.

- Investors who have bought shares listed on the Stockholm bourse this year have made big profits if they sold the shares as soon as they were listed. The losers are those who bought shares after they had listed hoping they would rise further.

- Ericsson is having problems with its mobile phones in Asia. Australia's biggest mobile operator, Telstra, has stopped selling Ericsson's tiny GF 788 model phone as it had operating problems. The newspaper said that Ericsson had been forced to recall 200,000 of the new model. This is giving competitors a chance to muscle into the market.

- The spread between Swedish and German long bonds has narrowed to less than one percent again. This is only the second time this has happened in the 1990s. On Thursday the difference was about 0.96 percent.
